3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within 30 days following each
  fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment balances. The purpose
  of the report is to inform, on a quarterly basis, the City’s cash and investment balances,
  the investment types, yields, and market values, and to ensure that the City’s investments
  are in compliance with the City’s adopted investment policy.

  Recommended Action
  Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local officials
  have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with
  COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
  protect the health and safely of attendees.

4.  Grant Funding Application to the California Division of Boating and Waterways
  The City of Avalon submitted a grant application on August 1, 2023 to the California
  Division of Boating and Waterways for a Tier I Boating Infrastructure Grant. Though the
  grant application was executed by the City Manager on August 1, 2023, the grant requires
  a resolution from the City Council designating the City Manager, or his designee, as an
  authorized signer.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution authorizing the application of grant funds from the California Division
  of Boating and Waterways Boating Infrastructure Grant, and authorize the City Manager,
  or their designee, to be the authorized signature on the grant application.

5.  Engineered Solution Group On-Call Engineering Services Contract Extension and
  Annual Increase
  In January 2020, the City Council authorized a professional services contract for on-call
  engineering with Engineered Solution Group (ESG). The City utilizes the services of ESG
  for various civil engineering services. Due to the COVID-19 Pandemic, the City delayed
  implementation of many CIP projects. The delay in implementation as well as the growing
  and varied nature of current, ongoing City projects, has caused an increase in the
  utilization of ESG services in 2023.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute an amendment to the City’s On-Call Engineering
  Professional Services Agreement with Engineered Solution Group, renewing the contract
  term for an additional two-year period effective January 1, 2024, and increasing the
  contracted maximum annual cumulative total for all services from $500,000 to $800,000
  effective immediately.

GENERAL BUSINESS

6.  Resolution Amending Memorandum of Understanding Between the City of Avalon and
  International Association of Firefighters Local 2295
  In May 2022, the City Council adopted Resolution 22-25 approving the Memorandum of
  Understanding (MOU) between the City and the International Association of Firefighters
  Local 2295 (Fire Union) effective July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025. Representatives
  from the Fire Union and the City Manager have held several meetings resulting in the
  mutual proposal of two amendments to the existing MOU agreement.

  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution amending the Memorandum of Understanding between the City of
  Avalon and the International Association of Firefighters Local 2295 for the contract period
  July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.

7.  Transient Rental License Discussion
  On August 1, 2023, the City Council voted unanimously to establish, by urgency
  ordinance, a moratorium on the issuance of Transient Rental Licenses for transient rental
  use to new applicants for a 45-day period. The moratorium was established to allow City
  Council, City Staff and the City Attorney time to study appropriate regulations to maintain
  public safety and health of the community.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss the Staff proposal for analyzing transient rental issues. Provide direction to Staff.

8.  Presentation and Discussion on Landlord Tenant Regulatory Options
  State law provides certain landlord tenant regulations throughout the state, but cities may
  enact additional regulations if they so choose.
  Recommended Action
  Consider existing landlord tenant regulations under state law, as well as City options for
  creating additional regulations, and direct Staff to prepare a tenant-landlord ordinance for
  future consideration if the Council deems it appropriate.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-1 9 state of emergency
proclaimed by the Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local
officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection
with COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
protect the health and safely of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. AB 361 provides an exception to these procedures in
order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including the COVID-1 9
pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required underAB 361

As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual meetings
without providing notice of the City Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes
the following two findings:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; and

  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and danger
  presented by COVID-19;

from the California Division of Boating and Waterways Boating Infrastructure Grant, and

REPORT SUMMARY: The City of Avalon submitted a grant application on August 1, 2023 to
the California Division of Boating and Waterways for a Tier I Boating Infrastructure Grant.
Though the grant application was executed by the City Manager on August 1, 2023, the grant
requires a resolution from the City Council designating the City Manager, or his designee. as an
authorized signer. The California Division of Boating and Waterways allows a grace period for
resolution to be submitted after the submission deadline.

The grant application is for a construction project to replace the Club Dinghy Dock pier, pilings,
ramp, and dock complex. The goal of this project is to replace the current aged and worn
infrastructure to improve public shore-access to recreational boaters.

The City applied for, and was awarded, funding through this grant program in 2017 for the
replacement of the Pump-out Float. That project was completed this past spring.

The grant program is comprised of 75% grant funds, 25% local match. The total project cost is
estimated to be $266,000. The City requested $199,500 in grant funds and the local match is
$66,500.

SUBJECT:  Engineered Solution Group On-Call Engineering Services Contract
  Extension and Annual Increase

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute an amendment to the
City’s On-Call Engineering Professional Services Agreement with Engineered Solution Group,
renewing the contract term for an additional two-year period effective January 1, 2024, and
increasing the contracted maximum annual cumulative total for all services from $500,000 to
$800,000 effective immediately.

REPORT SUMMAR’Y: On January 7, 2020, the City Council authorized the City Manager to
contract professional services for on-call engineering with Engineered Solution Group (ESG)
for a not to exceed annual amount of $500,000. The original contract term was from January 8,
2020 to December 31, 2023, with two additional one-year renewal terms.

The City has several Capital Improvement Program (CIP) projects and on-going maintenance
needs that occasionally require technical areas of service. The City utilizes the services of
ESG for various civil engineering services including, but not limited to design, review,
coordination, administration and construction engineering and technical support of day-to-day
Public Works operations of City Staff and Capital Improvement Projects.

Due to the COVID-19 Pandemic, the City delayed implementation of many CIP projects. The
delay in implementation as well as the growing and varied nature of current, ongoing City
projects, has caused an increase in the utilization of ESG services in 2023.

Many of the City’s projects have a specific timeline. In some cases, the need for services is of
limited scope and timeline, making it beneficial from a cost and timing perspective to have
someone “on-call.” Alternatively, a request for proposals for technical areas of engineering
services could be solicited for each project and task. This option requires additional time and
administrative preparation for each contract and can be cost prohibitive for certain projects that
have specific timelines or require immediate services.

Task orders for on-call services are driven by the approved budget. Annually funds cannot be
spent unless they are a part of an approved, budgeted, project or account or receive additional
City Council approval in accordance with the approved budget and fiscal policies of the budget.
Task orders related to grant funds may be eligible for reimbursement or payment through
grants, and are accounted for in the grant project’s budget.
 In order to continue to efficiently move CIP projects, and other maintenance programs,
forward, City Staff recommend the City Council authorizes the City Manager, or his designee,
to execute an amendment to the City’s On-Call Engineering Profes&onal Services Agreement
with Engineered Solution Group, renewing the contract term for an additional two-year period
effective January 1, 2024, and increasing the contracted maximum annual cumulative total for
all services from $500000 to $800,000 effective immediately.

The amendment will have negligible fiscal impact as all task orders associated with ESG’s
scope of work are approved and budgeted within the CIP and maintenance program.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Not to exceed S800,000 for all task orders per fiscal year for all approved
on-call engineer services, effective September 1, 2023. for an additional two year period
expiring December 31, 2025. Funding will be allocated to the appropriate budgeted project.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Efficient operations. Fiscal responsibility.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will need to
procure the engineering related services for each project and task order which may take more
time and cost additional funds.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

10.1.1 GENERAL
  Introduction
  A local agency may engage consultants to perform architectural, engineering, and related
  services to develop a federal-aid funded project. Local agencies requesting federal funds to
  reimburse A&E Consultants must follow the selection arid contracting procedures detailed in
  this chapter.

  Definition of an ArchiteCtural and Engineering Consultant
  23 Code of Federal Regulations §172 and CA State Law further defines A&E services and
  includes those private consulting firms providing architectural, landscape architectural,
  engineering, environmental, land surveying, construction engineering, or program
  management are termed Architectural and Engineering (A&E) Consultants.

  Architectural and Engineering Consultants
  The Brooks Act (40 USC, Section 1104) requires local agencies to award federally funded
  engineering and design related contracts based on fair and open competitive negotiations,
  demonstrated competence, and professional qualifications (23 Code of Federal Regulations
  (CFR), Fart 172), at a fair and reasonable price (48 CFR 31.201-3).
  Cost proposals submitted to the local agency must be sealed and shall not be included as a
  criterion for rating such consultants. After ranking, cost negotiations may begin with the most
  qualified consultant and only their cost proposal will be opened. Should negotiations fail or
  result in a price that the local agency does not consider fair and reasonable, negotiations must
  be formally terminated and the local agency must then undertake negotiations with the second
  most qualified consultant.
  If the negotiations with the second most qualified firm are not successful, negotiations must be
  formally terminated and the local agency must then undertake negotiations with the third most

  Consultants Performing Work on Multiple Phases of Federal-aid Projects
  Local agencies sometimes wish to hire the same consultant firm to perform construction
  engineering and/or inspection services on the same project on which the firm also performed
  design services. This can cause project delivery efficiencies, as the design firm is well-suited to
  verify that the project is being constructed in accordance with the design and can resolve issues
  related to the design on behalf of the contracting agency. However, this may also pose a
  potential conflict of interest if the firm has a vested financial interest in failing to disclose
  deficiencies in its design work product and seeks to insulate itself from pecuniary liability in
  subsequent phases of the project, such as minimizing or ignoring design errors and omissions,
  rather than serving the best interests of the contracting agency and the public. Procuring a
  different firm from the design firm to provide the construction engineering and/or inspection
  services provides another level of review and reduces the risk of, or potential for, a conflict of
  interest.

  Estimated Cost of Consultant Work
  An independent estimate for cost or price analysis is needed for all consultant contracts (23 CER
  172.7(a)(1)(v)(B)) to ensure that consultant services are obtained at a fair and reasonable price.
  tie estimate is prepared in advance of requesting a cost proposal from the top-ranked
  consultant, so the local agency’s negotiating team has a cost comparison of the project to
  evaluate the reasonableness of the consultant’s cost proposal. The estimate, which is specifically
  for the use of the local agency’s negotiating team, is to be kept confidential and maintained for
  records.
  A good cost estimate can be prepared only if the scope of work is defined clearly. The scope of
  work must include a list of the products or services which the consultant is required to deliver,
  and a time schedule of when they must be delivered.
  It should be stressed that all work to be decived from the consultant services, such as
  preliminary design, environmental or final design, must be clearly identified in the solicitation
  of consultant services (RFQ or REP) arid included in the cost estimate. The addition of work to
  the original scope by amendment should be avoided whenever possible. Contract modifications
  are required for any amendments to the terms of the existing contract that change the cost of the
  contract; significantly change the character, scope, complexity, or duration of the work; or
  significantly change the conditions under which the work is required to be performed.
  Some of the costs estimating techniques are:
  Analogous Estimating:
  Analogous cost estimating is using the actual cost of a previous, similar contract as the basis for
  estimating the cost of the current contract. Analogous cost estimating is frequently used to
  estimate costs when there is a limited amount of detailed information about the project.
  Analogous cost estimating is generally less accurate and it is most reliable when previous
  projects are similar in fact, and not just in appearance, and it uses expert judgment.
  Parametric Estimating:
  Parametric estimating is a technique that uses statistical relationship between historical data
  and other variables to calculate a cost estimate for an activity resource. This technique can
  produce a higher level of accuracy depending upon the sophistication, as well as underlying
  resource quantity and the cost data. A cost example would involve multiplying the planned
  quantity of work by the historical cost per unit to obtain the estimated cost of the contract.
  Bottom-up Estimating:
  This technique involves estimating the cost for individual work in the contract with the lowest
  level of detail. This detailed cost is then summarized or rolled up to determine a total cost of
  contract. Cost detail should include estimated hours per task, labor hourly cost for professional
  and non-professional classifications, subconsultant costs, other project direct costs, and profit.
  Labor costs should be broken down to direct labor and indirect cost rates, if possible.
  If more than one project or phase of work is to be developed within the consultant contract,
  separate cost estimates are required for each project or phase of work. Separate cost estimates
  are required for each milestone and portion of the work expected to be subcontracted.

  Actual Cost-Plus-Fixed Fee
  The consultant is reimbursed for actual costs incurred and receives an additional predetermined
  amount as a fixed fee (profit). Federal regulations require that profit be separately negotiated
  from contract costs. The determination of the amount of the fixed fee shall take into account the
  size, complexity, duration, and degree of risk involved in the work. The fixed fee is not
  adjustable during the life of the contract. The fixed fee dollar amount must be clearly stated in
  the contract.
  This method of payment is appropriate when the extent, scope, complexity, character, or
  duration of work cannot be precisely predicted. The fixed fee limit applies to the total direct and
  indirect costs. Fixed fees in excess of 15 percent of the total direct labor and indirect costs of the
  contract may be justified only when exceptional circumstances exist. The contract shall specify a
  reasonable maximum length of contract period and a maximum total contract dollar amount
  (see Exhibit 10-H; Sample Cost Proposal Example #1 and Exhibit 10-R: A&E Sample Contract
  Language, Article V, Option i in this chapter). The contract cost proposal must identify all key
  employees and/or classifications to be billed. New key employees and/or classifications must
  be approved before they incur work on the contract or the costs can be questioned or
  disallowed.

Bilingual Pay

The existing MOU had a provision granting an additional $25 per month to qualified bilingual
employees that routinely provide translation services when speaking with the public. The
Parties discussed an increase the bilingual pay allowance from $25 per month to $100 per
month.

The nature of translation services used by members of the Fire Union is much higher level
than in other areas of City service. Qualified union members translate vital healthcare
information in emergency situations. In some cases, due to the level of translation, more
fluent union members are called during emergency situations to provide translation services
when not on shift. The level of service and resulting quality of care is significant.

The proposed addendum authorizes the monthly increase for qualified employees
designated by the Fire Chief. The pay will be considered special Assignment Pay and shall
be reported as such pursuant to Title 2CRR, Section 571 (a) (2).

limited redundancy, the need exists to expand the pool of employees that are qualified to
 Additionally, by allowing qualified employees to garner field experience as an Acting
Captain, employees will have better understanding of the activities and responsibilities of
the higher position, and may be more prepared for a potential promotion should a vacancy

SUBJECT:  Transient Rental License Discussion

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Discuss the Staff proposal for analyzing transient rental
issues. Provide direction to Staff.

REPORT SUMMARY: On August 1, 2023, the City Council voted unanimously to establish, by
urgency ordinance, a moratorium on the issuance of Transient Rental Licenses for transient
rental use to new applicants for a 45-day period. The 45-day period expires on September 14,
2023.

The moratorium was established to allow City Council, Planning Commission, City Staff and
the City Attorney time to study appropriate regulations to maintain public safety and health of
the community. Additionally, the moratorium will temporarily halt further issuance of TRLs so
that the City can identify regulations which ensure that issuance of TRLs does not undermine
the City’s goals to have affordable housing stock and maintain a safe community.

City Staff propose a series of three stakeholder/community meetings to discuss specific issues
regarding transient rentals:
  -  Tuesday, September 22 at 5 p.m. Meeting to discuss quality of life issues, specifically
  —

  noise, trash, and other community impacts.
  -  Wednesday, September 30 at 5 p.m.  —  Meeting to discuss financial benefits and
  impacts, sustainability and housing impacts.
  -  Saturday, date and time TBD Meeting to summarize current findings and discussion of
  —

  regulatory processes.

In addition, to the proposed stakeholder/community meetings, City Staff are developing a
community survey. A preliminary draft of the survey is included with this report. The
stakeholder/community meetings will help Staff refine survey questions. Staff anticipate
circulating the survey for a 30-day period, not to coincide with the already scheduled
Community-Wide Survey.

Currently, the City is addressing all factors that negatively impact long term housing stock, with
an emphasis on affordable housing, and has received complaints from property owners of the
negative impacts that result from living in close proximity to property that has been granted
either a CUP or TRL for transient rental uses. Specifically, the City has received numerous
 complaints in the form of public comment about noise impacts, traffic impacts! and safety
impacts to residents relating to issuance of CUPs and TRLs.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION:  The City’s existing
rules for the granting of transient occupancy licenses will remain in place.

SUBJECT:  Presentation and Discussion on Landlord Tenant Regulatory Options

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Consider existing landlord tenant regulations under state law,
as well as City options for creating additional regulations, and direct Staff to prepare a tenant-
landlord ordinance for future consideration if the Council deems it appropriate.

REPORT SUMMARY: State law provides certain landlord tenant regulations throughout the
state, but cities may enact additional regulations if they so choose. The report summarizes
current state regulations and discussions other regulations cities have enacted.

California’s Tenant Protections

California’s Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (“TPA”) prevents a landlord from evicting tenants
without “just cause.” Just cause may be ‘at-fault” or “no-fault.” At-fault just cause allows the
landlord to evict and provide little to no assistance. But no-fault just cause requires the landlord
to provide assistance to the evicted renter (even though the landlord still gets to evict).’

At-fault
“At-fault” just causes include: default in payment of rent, breach of a material term, nuisance,
waste, refusal to sign a new lease, criminal activity, unauthorized assignment or subletting,
refusing entry to landlord, using the property for an unlawful purpose, and termination of
employment if employee housing.

No-fault
“No-fault” just causes include: use of the unit by the owner’s family; withdrawal of the unit from
the rental market; a court or other government order to vacate the property; and “intent to
demolish or to substantially remodel” the unit. With no-fault just cause, the landlord must pay
relocation assistance equal to one month rent, regardless of tenant income.

Exemptions
The TPA does not apply to a short-term rental or hotel; housing for a nonprofit hospital, religious
facility, or various care facilities; school dorms; owner-occupied housing (sharing kitchen or
bathroom with owner); single-family owner-occupied residences; an owner-occupied duplex;
housing built within the last 15 years (except for mobile homes); housing that is separately

Floor, not ceiling.
The TPA sets the floor for new tenant protections; it does not prevent a city from adopting

The TPA does not apply to properties that are subject to a local ordinance that requires just

TPA even if the TPA is more strict.)

Nor does the TPA apply to properties that are subject to a newer local ordinance (post-
September 2019)— as long as the ordinance is at least as protective as the TPA

Summarizing the TPA
The statewide IPA provides some benefits (one-month’s rent for relocation) in some situations
(specific enumerated no-fault evictions). It does not prevent eviction. It allows eviction for a major
remodel. And it doesn’t apply to several types of housing.

Avalon has no local tenant-protection ordinance, so any ordinance that it might adopt must be
at least as protective as the TPA.

Options for Additional Local Protections

Many California cities adopt local regulations to provide additional protections for renters. These
additional protections tend to be the following:
  • Eliminating or narrowing certain just causes (e.g., not allowing “major remodel” as a no-
  fault just cause).
  • Increasing relocation assistance (e.g., three or four months’ worth of rent).
  • Expanding the protections to other types of dwellings (e.g., eliminating exemption for
  newer homes).
  • Imposing rent control.
  • Create rent registry and rent-control board to consider exceptions to rent-control
  restrictions.

long as they are at least as protective as the TPA.
